passages.title: The clear Book: guidance and warning
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the doorway into Sūrah an-Naml. They do one thing, in one connected movement: they name what this Book is, name the people who actually benefit from it, name the people who are shut out from it and why, and finally name the One it is coming from. Notice the frame — ayah 1 begins with *"These are the verses of the Quran; the clear Book"* and ayah 6 ends with *"you are being taught the Qur'an from One, All-Wise, All-Knowing."* The passage opens with the Book and closes with its Sender, and everything in between is the two kinds of hearts that meet it. Ibn Kathir gathers the whole unit under a single heading: **"The Qur'an is Guidance and Glad Tidings for the Believers, a Warning to the Disbelievers, and it is from Allah."**

## Ṭā Sīn — and the discipline of not guessing

The sūrah opens with the letters **Ṭā Sīn**. It is worth noticing what Ibn Kathir does here: he does not offer an interpretation at all. He simply says, **"In (the comments on) Surat Al-Baqarah, we discussed the letters which appear at the beginning of some Surahs"** — and moves on.

That restraint is itself instructive. A believer is not required to have an opinion about every secret in the Book; some things are received before they are explained. And notice what follows immediately: these letters, and then the declaration that what stands here is *"the verses of the Quran; the clear Book."*

## "These are the verses… the clear Book"

Ayah 1 gives the revelation two names: the **Qur'an**, and a **Book that is clear** — *kitāb mubīn*. Ibn Kathir's gloss on that last word is exactly two words: **"It is plain and evident."**

That deserves a pause. This is not a riddle-book, not a coded oracle. Whatever difficulty a reader has with it, Ibn Kathir's verdict stands: it is plain and evident. Which already sets up the whole problem the rest of the passage will unfold — if the Book is plain, then when someone fails to see, the failure lies somewhere other than in the light.

## Guidance and good news — and the condition attached (ayat 2–3)

Ayah 2 calls the Qur'an **"a guide and good news for the believers."** The obvious question is why guidance is restricted to believers, when guidance is precisely what a person needs *in order* to believe.

Ibn Kathir answers by describing the transaction rather than the label. Guidance and good news, he says, **"may be attained from the Qur'an for those who believe in it, follow it and put it into practice."** Three verbs, in that order: believe, follow, act. The Qur'an is not a substance that works on a passive reader. It gives its light to the one who leans into it.

This is why he sets alongside it the ayah from Sūrah Fuṣṣilat: *"Say: 'It is for those who believe, a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness (deafness) in their ears…'"* (41:44) — one and the same recitation, and the difference in outcome is in the listener. He also cites *"that you may give glad tidings to those who have Taqwa, and warn with it the Ludd (most quarrelsome) people"* (19:97): the same Book, arriving as glad tidings at one door and as warning at another.

Then ayah 3 refuses to leave "believer" as an unexamined word, and defines it by three things:

**1. They establish the prayer.** Ibn Kathir specifies **"obligatory prayers."** Not prayer as a mood or an occasional impulse — the appointed, repeating obligation.

**2. They give the zakāh.** Faith that reaches the wealth. The first mark disciplines the body and the day; the second disciplines the pocket, which for most of us is the harder of the two.

**3. They have sure faith in the Hereafter.** Here Ibn Kathir unpacks what such certainty actually contains, because it is not a vague sense that something follows death. It is belief **"with certain faith in the Hereafter, the resurrection after death, reward and punishment for all deeds, good and bad, and Paradise and Hell."** Four things: that the dead are raised; that every deed is answered for; that the answer runs in both directions, reward and punishment; and Paradise and Hell.

There is a quiet logic in the ordering too. Prayer and zakāh are visible actions; certainty about the Hereafter is the invisible conviction underneath them that makes the two worth doing. The passage is about to show what happens to a life when that invisible foundation is missing.

## The hinge of the passage: denying the Hereafter (ayah 4)

Ayah 4 turns, and it turns on exactly the item ayah 3 ended with. The believers were described as having sure faith in the Hereafter; now: *"As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter…"* Ibn Kathir specifies who is meant — **"those who deny it and think that it will never happen."** Not people troubled by doubt, but people settled in denial.

And what follows is one of the more sobering statements in the Qur'an: **"We have made their deeds fair seeming to them, so that they wander about blindly."**

## "We made their deeds fair-seeming": how the scholars read it

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that the commentators took *zayyannā lahum aʿmālahum* in two ways.

**The first reading** — the one Maʿārif itself judges **"more appropriate and straightforward"** — is that *their deeds* here means their **bad** actions: Allah made their bad actions look adorned in their sight, so, in Maʿārif's words, **"they feel good about them and remain enthralled in depravity."** That is the terror of it: not a person who knows he is doing wrong and does it anyway, but a person whose wrongdoing has been dressed up until it looks to him like something fine.

**The second reading**, which Maʿārif attributes to "some commentators," takes *their deeds* to mean **good** deeds — that Allah **"had placed the good deeds before them with all their attractions. But those unjust people did not pay any attention to them, rather they remained engrossed in infidelity; hence lost their way in wilderness."**

Maʿārif gives two reasons for preferring the first. **One**, Qur'anic usage: the word *zīnah*, adornment, **"has been generally used for bad actions"** — *"It has been made attractive for people to love the desires"* (3:14); *"Adorned is the present life for those who disbelieve"* (2:212); and again in 6:137. Its use for good actions is, it says, "very rare," as in *"But Allah has endeared to you belief, decking it fair in your hearts"* (49:7). **Two**, the wording itself: the phrase is *their* deeds, and Maʿārif holds that this too points to bad actions being meant here rather than righteous ones.

Ibn Kathir, for his part, paraphrases the ayah: **"'We have made what they are doing seem good to them, and We have left them to continue in their misguidance, so they are lost and confused.'"** Then comes his decisive sentence: **"This is their recompense for their disbelief in the Hereafter."**

That word — *recompense* — is where a reader should slow down. What the ayah describes is a requital: they first refused, and this came after, as the answer to their refusal. Ibn Kathir proves it from the Qur'an itself: *"And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe therein for the first time"* (6:110) — note "for the first time." The first turning away was theirs; what followed was consequence.

The end of ayah 4 gives the result: **"so that they wander about blindly."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is **"lost and confused."** Picture a man in open country walking with total confidence and no direction — the confidence is precisely the disease. He is not paralysed; he is busy, active, pleased with himself. He simply has no idea where he is.

## The greatest losers (ayah 5)

Ayah 5 states the outcome in two time-frames. **"They are those for whom there will be an evil torment"** — and Ibn Kathir specifies its scope: **"in this world and the Hereafter."** The misery is not postponed in its entirety; a life spent wandering blindly is already a punished life, and the punishment of the next world is added to it.

Then: **"and in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers."** Not merely losers — the greatest. Ibn Kathir spells out what that means on the day all people are gathered: **"no one but they, among all the people who will be gathered, will lose their souls and their wealth."**

Read that against ayah 3 and the passage snaps into focus. The believers gave: they gave their time to the prayer and their wealth to the zakāh, and might have thought they were spending. The deniers kept everything, and are the ones who end up with nothing — not their wealth, not even themselves.

## "You are receiving the Qur'an" (ayah 6)

Having laid out the two responses, the passage closes by going back behind the Book to its Source, addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir notes that **"And verily, you"** means **"O Muhammad"** — *"are being taught the Qur'an from One, All-Wise, All-Knowing."*

On the phrase **"are being taught,"** Ibn Kathir cites **Qatadah**, who explained it with one word: **"Are receiving."** That is a precise and important gloss. The Prophet ﷺ is on the receiving end. He is not composing, not editing, not selecting — he is being handed something.

Then the two divine descriptions that end the passage, which Ibn Kathir treats together. The Qur'an comes **"from One Who is Wise in His commands and prohibitions, and Who knows all things, major and minor."**

- **Ḥakīm, All-Wise** — Ibn Kathir ties this to His commands and prohibitions: what this Book instructs and what it forbids comes from wisdom.
- **ʿAlīm, All-Knowing** — He **"knows all things, major and minor."** Nothing, great or small, is outside His knowledge.

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion tightly: **"Whatever He says is absolute Truth, and His rulings are entirely fair and just,"** and he anchors it in the ayah *"And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice"* (6:115).

And this is the answer to ayah 4. If the Book is plain and evident, and its Sender is All-Knowing and All-Wise, then when a man reads it and remains lost, we know exactly where the fault does not lie.

## A note on the surrounding context

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, commenting at the close of the previous sūrah (on 26:224, so just outside our passage), records that **the pagans of Makkah used to call the Prophet ﷺ a *shāʿir* (poet) and the Qur'an *shiʿr* (poetry)** — and that on one scholarly view they meant this in the word's literal sense, since *shiʿr* lexically means **"any statement based on imagination and ideas not confirmed by serious proofs."** Maʿārif is blunt about the intent: **"Their objective was to call him a liar."** Hold that beside ayah 1 and ayah 6: against *made-up thoughts*, this Book calls itself plain and evident; against *he is inventing it*, ayah 6 says he is **receiving** it — from the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.

## Living it

**Test your claim to guidance by Ibn Kathir's three verbs.** Guidance is attained by the one who *believes in it, follows it, and puts it into practice*. Recitation without following, and following without practice, do not draw down the light. If the Qur'an is not changing anything, the question to ask is which of the three is missing.

**Take ayah 3 as a checklist, in its own order.** The prayer established as an obligation, not a mood. The zakāh actually paid. And sure faith in the Hereafter — resurrection, reward and punishment for deeds good and bad, Paradise and Hell. Weakness in the third quietly erodes the first two, because the first two only make sense if the third is true.

**Be suspicious of a settled contentment with your own conduct.** The most frightening thing in ayah 4 is not that these people sin, but that their sin *looks good to them*. A conscience that never objects is not necessarily a clean conscience. This is precisely why the Book had to come from outside us: a measure we did not write is the only thing that can correct the eyes we judge with.

**And take comfort from ayah 6 when the Book is hard.** What you are reading comes from One who is Wise in His commands and prohibitions and who knows all things, major and minor. Nothing in it is arbitrary, and nothing in it is uninformed.

passages.title: Moses at the fire, and Pharaoh's knowing denial
passages.tafsir:
A man lost in the dark goes looking for a burning stick to warm his family, and comes back a Prophet. That is the hinge of this passage: ayat 7–12 tell how Allah called Musa (peace be upon him) at the fire and armed him with signs, and ayat 13–14 tell what Pharaoh's court did with those signs — rejected them out loud while knowing, inwardly, that they were true. Ibn Kathir frames the whole unit as Allah informing His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ of how He chose Musa, spoke with him, gave him mighty and dazzling proofs, and sent him to Pharaoh and his people — who denied the proof and arrogantly refused to follow. Guidance offered, guidance refused: that is the thread.

## A cold night and a lost road (ayah 7)

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Musa was travelling with his family, at night, in the dark, and had lost his way. He noticed a fire burning brightly beside the mountain.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that he faced two needs at once — to find the road he had lost, and to get warm, because it was a cold night. And notice how he speaks. He does not claim success in his errand; his words convey servanthood and hope in Allah. He says "I will bring you some information" and "perhaps you may warm yourselves." Maʿārif draws the lesson: to strive and take practical steps for one's needs is not opposed to *tawakkul* — trust and reliance placed in Allah. What matters is where the conviction sits: in Allah, not in one's own effort. Maʿārif adds an observation from Rūḥ: perhaps the wisdom in showing him a fire specifically is that one thing answered both needs — light to find the way, and heat to warm them.

Two small details repay attention, both noted by Maʿārif:

**He speaks to one person in the plural.** Maʿārif points to two words Musa used in the plural form — *umkuthū* ("wait!", from the telling of this same night in Sūrah Ṭā Hā, 20:10, which Maʿārif places alongside our ayah) and *taṣṭalūn* ("that you may warm yourselves"). Plural forms are used where the addressees are more than one, yet the only person with him was his wife, the daughter of Shuʿayb (peace be upon him). Maʿārif explains this as a mark of respect to her, the way dignified people sometimes address a single person in the plural. It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ likewise used to address his wives in the plural form.

**He says "my family," not her name.** The word *ahl* means household and covers everyone under one's roof, though here his wife was the only one present. Maʿārif takes this as a hint of *adab* — the fine manners Islam teaches: when referring to one's wife in a gathering, it is better to use a general expression — "my family members are of the opinion" — rather than naming her.

Two ordinary courtesies, embedded in a moment of crisis. The man was cold, lost, and about to be addressed by his Lord, and the Qur'an still preserves how carefully he spoke of his wife.

## The fire that was not a fire (ayah 8)

What he found was not what he expected. Ibn Kathir describes the scene: he saw a great and terrifying sight — the fire was burning in a green bush, and the fire blazed ever brighter while the bush grew ever more green and beautiful. He raised his head and saw its light joined to the clouds of the sky. Ibn ʿAbbās and others said it was not fire at all, but shining light; in one report from Ibn ʿAbbās, it was the Light of the Lord of the worlds. Musa stood amazed at what he was seeing — and then the call came.

**"Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it."** *Būrika* — Ibn ʿAbbās glossed it: *Holy is* whoever is in the fire. Who is meant? The commentators differ, and both tafsirs record the disagreement honestly:

- *Whoever is around it* means the angels — the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, as Ibn Kathir reports.
- Maʿārif reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah that *whoever is in the fire* is Musa himself — because what he saw was not real fire, but a blessed spot so luminous that from a distance it looked like fire; so Musa, standing in that light, was "in the fire," and the angels present nearby were "around it."
- Other commentators reverse it: those *in* the fire are the angels, and the one *around* it is Musa. Maʿārif notes that Tafsīr Bayān ul-Qurʼān adopts this second reading, and adds that knowing this much is enough for the meaning of these verses.

### A boundary the passage itself draws

There is a third narration, and Maʿārif handles it with great care because a careless reading would wreck one's belief. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardūyah and others report from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that *whoever is in the fire* refers to Allah Himself. Maʿārif's response is firm: fire is created by Allah, and it is impossible for the Creator to enter into anything He created. This narration can never mean that Allah became the fire, in the way idol-worshippers believe their gods take form in their idols — that is flatly against tawḥīd, the Oneness of Allah. What is meant is manifestation, like a reflection in a mirror: the image appears in the mirror, but the thing itself is not inside the mirror; what you see there exists outside it, with its own reality.

Maʿārif then closes the door further. This was not a showing of Allah's own Self, because Musa afterwards asked at Mount Ṭūr, *"My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You"* (7:143) — a request that would make no sense had he already seen it, and the answer *lan tarānī*, "You will never see Me," would be meaningless. That reply also makes clear that in this world no one can witness the refulgence of His real Self. Maʿārif calls what happened here a figurative manifestation, of the kind commonly spoken of among the mystics, admits it is difficult to comprehend fully, and refers the reader to the author's Arabic work *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* on Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the same ayah guards the same frontier from the other side. On *"And glorified be Allah, the Lord of all that exists"* he writes: He does whatever He wills, and there is nothing like Him among His creation. Nothing He has made can encompass Him; He is the Exalted, the Almighty, utterly unlike all that He has created. Heaven and earth cannot contain Him; He is the One, the Self-Sufficient Master, far above any comparison with His creation.

**Why the tasbīḥ is here at all.** Maʿārif makes a sharp point: in a situation like this — a voice heard from a burning tree — people are normally led into confusion and end up in idol worship. So in every place the Qur'an tells this story, the Oneness of Allah is reminded and emphasised alongside. Here it is *"and glorified be Allah, the Lord of the worlds"* (27:8). In Ṭā Hā it is *"there is no god but I"* (20:14). In al-Qaṣaṣ it is *"I am Allah, Lord of the worlds"* (28:30). The conclusion Maʿārif draws is worth memorising: the fire was shown to Musa because he was in need of fire and light that night, and there is otherwise no connection between the Word of Allah, or the Being of Allah, and that fire or that tree of Ṭūr. Fire was nothing but a creature of Allah, like so many other creatures.

## "It is I — Allah" (ayah 9)

Ibn Kathir: Allah told him that the One addressing him was his Lord, Allah, al-ʿAzīz — the All-Mighty, who has subjugated and subdued all things — al-Ḥakīm, the One who is Wise in all His words and deeds. Those are the two names under which the sender introduces Himself, on the night He commissions His Messenger.

Maʿārif places this ayah beside the parallels — *"It is Me, your Lord"* (20:12), *"I am Allah, there is no god but I"* (20:14), *"I am Allah, Lord of the worlds"* (28:30) — and says it is possible that this call was repeated again and again, sometimes in one wording and then another.

On *how* it was heard, Maʿārif cites Abū Ḥayyān in *Tafsīr al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ* and al-Ālūsī in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: it was heard as though emanating from all sides, and not from any particular direction; and it was received not by the ears alone but by every part of his body — itself nothing less than a miracle. It was the sound of an invisible Speaker, heard without a particular quality (*kayf*, the "how") and without determining a direction, though its source was the fire, or the tree on which the fire was glowing. This is the classical instinct: affirm that Allah spoke, and refuse to specify the *how*.

## The staff, and a fear that is allowed (ayat 10–11)

Then came the command: **throw down your staff.** Ibn Kathir explains the purpose — so that Allah might show him clear proof that He is the One able to do all things, whatever He wills. Musa threw it, and it changed into the form of a huge and terrifying snake, moving quickly despite its size.

The Arabic is precise. *Jānn*, Ibn Kathir notes, refers to a type of snake that is the fastest-moving and most agile — so the picture is of something huge moving with the quickness of the nimblest kind. And of *wallā mudbiran wa lam yuʿaqqib*, Ibn Kathir says simply: he did not turn around, because he was so afraid.

Then the reassurance: *"O Musa, fear not; the Messengers fear not before Me."* Ibn Kathir renders the sense: do not be afraid of what you see, for I want to choose you as a Messenger and make you a great Prophet. Fear is a natural human response; prophethood does not abolish the body's flinch, but the One who is speaking removes its ground.

### The exception in ayah 11

Maʿārif raises the question plainly. The miracle of the staff is mentioned in the ayah before this one, and the miracle of the shining hand in the ayah after it — so why is this exception placed between two verses about miracles, and is the exception *munqaṭiʿ* (snapped off from what precedes, so that "except" functions as "however") or *muttaṣil* (genuinely joined to the preceding statement)? The commentators hold different views:

- **If snapped off:** the previous ayah said the Messengers do not become frightened; this then mentions, in passing, who *does* have cause to fear — those who committed some sin, then repented, sought Allah's pardon and performed good deeds. Allah would pardon their sins, yet the possibility remains that some traces of the sin are left over, and for that reason such people always remain fearful of Allah.
- **If joined:** the meaning becomes that Allah's Messengers do not become frightened except one who committed some trifling or minor mistake and repented of it — and such slips are forgiven. Maʿārif immediately qualifies this: the actual position is that even the minor slips of the Messengers were not regarded as sins, neither small nor great; they looked like sins but were in fact errors of *ijtihād* (a judgement reached by sincere reasoning that turned out mistaken). On this reading the exception alludes to the incident of the Egyptian whom Musa killed by an error of judgement — pardoned by Allah, yet its effect remained with him, leaving some fear that would not otherwise have been there.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as an exception of the exclusionary type and draws out its gift for the rest of us: this is good news for mankind — whoever does an evil deed, then gives it up, repents and turns to Allah, Allah will accept his repentance. He cites *"And verily I am indeed forgiving to him who repents, believes and does righteous good deeds, and then is guided"* (20:82) and *"And whoever does evil or wrongs himself..."* (4:110), noting that many other ayat say the same.

Sit with the placement. At the very moment a man is being handed world-shaking miracles, the mention of forgiveness is inserted — as if to say that the door of return is never closed, not even in the middle of a scene about power.

## The shining hand, and two of nine (ayah 12)

**"Put your hand into the opening of your garment; it will come forth white without hurt."** Ibn Kathir: this is another sign, further brilliant proof of Allah's ability to do whatever He wills, and also confirmation of the truth of the one to whom the miracle was given. He put his hand in, took it out again, and it came out white and shining as if it were a piece of the moon or a flash of dazzling lightning.

*"Among the nine signs"* — Ibn Kathir explains: these are two of the nine signs with which you will be supported and which will serve as proof for you; the same nine referred to in *"And indeed We gave Musa nine clear signs"* (17:101).

And the destination: *"to Pharaoh and his people; verily, they are a people who are rebellious."* Their character is announced before Musa even arrives.

## Knowing, and denying anyway (ayat 13–14)

Now the passage turns, and its most searching statement arrives.

*"But when Our signs came to them, clear to see"* — Ibn Kathir glosses *mubṣirah* as clear and obvious — *"they said: this is manifest magic."* Ibn Kathir notes what came next: they wanted to oppose it with their own magic, but they were defeated and were returned disgraced.

Then ayah 14, which is the heart of the passage:

**"And they belied them"** — *jaḥadū*, which Ibn Kathir glosses in one word: verbally.

**"though they themselves were convinced thereof"** — *wastayqanat-hā anfusuhum*. Ibn Kathir: they knew deep down that this was the truth from Allah, but they denied it and were stubborn and arrogant. This is the difference between the ignorant and the obstinate. Their problem was never a shortage of evidence. The evidence had already landed and been accepted inwardly; the mouth simply refused to say what the self had settled.

**"wrongfully and arrogantly"** — *ẓulman wa ʿuluwwan*. Ibn Kathir separates the two: they wronged themselves, because this was the despicable manner to which they were accustomed; and they were arrogant, because they were too proud to follow the truth. One is habit, the other is pride — and together they are enough to make a person argue against something he already knows is true.

**"So see what was the end of the mischief-makers."** Ibn Kathir addresses the imperative to the Prophet ﷺ: see, O Muhammad, what the consequences of their actions were, when Allah destroyed them and drowned every last one of them in a single morning. The verb is *look* — the whole story has been building to a scene you are told to go and inspect.

## Why this story is told

Ibn Kathir states the point of the whole account without softening it: beware, O you who disbelieve in Muhammad and deny the Message he has brought from his Lord, lest the same thing that befell them befall you also. And he presses the comparison — what is worse is that Muhammad ﷺ is nobler and greater than Musa, and his proof stronger, for the signs Allah has given him are combined with his presence and his character, in addition to the fact that previous Prophets foretold his coming and took a covenant from their peoples that they would follow him if they should see him. May the best of blessings and peace from his Lord be upon him.

## What to carry away

- **Take the means, trust the Giver.** Musa went out looking for a burning ember. Striving for one's needs is not a rival to *tawakkul*, trust in Allah; misplaced confidence is. Keep the conviction in Allah, not in your own effort.
- **Guard your tongue about your household.** Two features of prophetic speech carry two courtesies — the plural of respect, and the discretion of saying "my family" rather than naming one's wife in company.
- **Keep the Creator and the created apart.** However luminous the sign, the tree is a tree and the fire is a creature of Allah. That is precisely why *subḥān Allāh* stands in the middle of the greatest moment of Musa's life.
- **Denial is often a decision, not a conclusion.** Pharaoh's people were convinced inwardly and refused anyway. Before assuming someone needs more argument, ask whether what is wanted is a reason to submit rather than a reason to believe — and ask it of yourself first.
- **The door stands open.** In the middle of thunder and serpents, Allah pauses to say: whoever wronged, then replaced evil with good — *I am Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful*.

passages.title: David and Solomon's knowledge, and the ant
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open the story of Sulayman (Solomon), peace be upon him, by telling us what Allah gave him and his father Dawud (David), peace be upon him — and then showing us, in one small incident on a march, what that gift actually looked like in a prophet's heart. Ibn Kathir frames the whole passage this way: Allah is telling us about the great blessings He bestowed on two of His servants and Prophets, father and son, who enjoyed happiness in this world and the Hereafter, power and authority on earth, and the rank of prophethood and messengership.

What holds the five ayat together is a single thread: **a gift is named, and immediately answered with praise.** In ayah 15 knowledge is given and the two prophets say *al-hamdu lillah*. In ayah 16 the inheritance and the language of the birds are given, and Sulayman calls it "an evident grace" from Allah. In ayah 17 the armies are gathered. In ayah 18 an ant speaks. And in ayah 19 the man riding at the head of hosts of jinn, men and birds, having understood a single insect, asks Allah for the ability to be grateful. The passage begins with knowledge and ends with humility, and the ant is the hinge between them.

## Ayah 15: knowledge is named first

"And indeed We gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman." Of everything Allah could have listed — the kingdom, the wind, the jinn, the birds — knowledge is what He mentions first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qurtubi, draws the lesson plainly: while relating all these graces, knowledge is mentioned first, and that is a clear hint that knowledge is the superior and paramount blessing among them all.

What knowledge? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it was obviously the special knowledge normally given to prophets about their functions and obligations as prophets — but it may also include other sciences and arts, since Dawud was given the art of making armour. So this is not knowledge sealed off from the world; it includes the practical craft by which a community is protected.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes what set these two apart among the prophets: they were given an empire alongside prophethood, and an empire of a very special nature — they ruled not only over human beings but over jinn and animals as well.

**And notice the response.** The ayah does not report that they enjoyed the gift; it reports what they *said*: "All praise be to Allah, Who has preferred us above many of His believing servants." The praise goes back to the Giver in the same breath in which the gift is mentioned. That reflex — receiving and immediately returning — is what the rest of the passage will test in the valley of the ants.

## Ayah 16: what a prophet leaves behind

"And Sulayman inherited from Dawud." Ibn Kathir is emphatic that this means inheritance **in kingship and prophethood**, not in wealth. His argument is twofold. First, the text singles Sulayman out; had wealth been meant, he would not have been singled out from among Dawud's sons, for Dawud had a hundred wives. Second, the wealth of the Prophets is not inherited at all, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"We Prophets cannot be inherited from; whatever we leave behind is charity."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same case and adds two supports. It cites the hadith reported by **Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud** from Sayyidnā Abū Dardāʾ (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said the *ʿulamāʾ* — the people of knowledge — are the inheritors of the prophets; the prophets did not leave dirhams or dinars as their legacy, but left knowledge as their heritage. And it argues rationally: when Dawud died he had nineteen sons, so if property were meant, every one of them would have had a claim; the inheritance described here is one his brothers were not included in, which can only be the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood. Along with it, Maʿārif adds, Allah graced Sulayman with Dawud's empire and, beyond that, with control over the jinn, the birds, the animals and the wind.

(Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions in passing that even al-Kulaini, the well-known Shiite scholar, reports from Jaʿfar as-Sadiq that Sulayman was the inheritor of Dawud and the Prophet ﷺ the inheritor of Sulayman — which, the commentary observes, can only mean an inheritance of knowledge, since no one can claim the Prophet ﷺ inherited Sulayman's property. On that basis it holds the contrary narration of Tabrasi, treating the inheritance as wealth, to be mistaken.)

For a placing in time, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from Qurtubi that seventeen hundred years separated the death of Sulayman from the birth of the last of the prophets, the Prophet ﷺ — Jewish reckoning puts it at fourteen hundred — and that Sulayman's own lifespan was a little over fifty years.

### "We have been taught the language of birds"

Two features of Sulayman's announcement repay attention.

**First, the plural.** He says *ʿullimnā* — "*we* have been taught" — though he was one man. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as a regal idiom: he used the plural of his office, to impress his subjects so that they would not grow slack in obeying Allah and in following him. From this the commentary derives a general permission: there is no harm in rulers and officials using the plural of themselves before those they govern, **provided it is for the esteem of the office and not out of arrogance.** The condition is the whole point — the same words can be either an instrument of order or a symptom of vanity, and only the heart behind them decides which.

**Second, why "birds" in particular.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes in a Special Note that the expression "speech of the birds" is used here because of the incident of the hoopoe, which is a bird; otherwise Sulayman was taught the languages of all the beasts, birds and insects — as the very next ayah shows, where he understands the speech of an ant. Ibn Kathir underlines how singular this was: he knew the speech of birds and animals, "something that had never been given to any other human being — as far as we know from what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ told us." Allah enabled him to understand what the birds said to one another as they flew, and what the different kinds of animals said. Maʿārif adds that Qurtubi records incidents in which Sulayman told people how the different birds chirped and what they meant by it — and that the chirping of each bird was a word of advice.

**"And we have been given of everything."** Read flatly, this claim is impossible — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses it directly with a point of Arabic usage. The word *kull* ("every, all") sometimes covers a whole category without limit, and sometimes its application is not universal but pertains to a specific purpose. Here it is the second: "everything" means only those things needed by a government or an empire. Obviously, the commentary notes drily, they had no aeroplanes, motor cars or railways in those days. Ibn Kathir reads the phrase the same way — "all things that a king needs." This is a useful habit of reading: Qur'anic universals are read within the frame the context sets, not stretched past it.

Sulayman closes: "This, verily, is an evident grace" — which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as, *this is clearly the blessing of Allah upon us.* Even the public proclamation of his own privilege ends by naming the Source.

## Ayah 17: the army, and the word that will come back

"And there were gathered before Sulayman his hosts of jinn and men and birds, and they all were set in battle order." Ibn Kathir pictures the scene: all of his troops of jinn, men and birds were gathered together, and he rode with them in a display of might and glory — people marching behind him, the jinn behind them, the birds flying above his head; and when it was hot, they would shade him with their wings.

Then the phrase *fa-hum yūzaʿūn*. Ibn Kathir explains that the first and the last of them were brought together so that none would step out of place, and quotes **Mujahid**: officials were appointed to keep each group in order, and to keep the first and the last together, so that no one would step out of line — "just as kings do nowadays."

Hold on to that verb. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *wazʿ*, which lexically means **to stop or to restrain**. The army is not merely organised; it is *restrained* — the sheer number would otherwise dissolve into confusion, so a check is placed on it. Two ayat later, Sulayman will ask Allah for exactly this same thing, for his own soul.

## Ayah 18: an ant, and a fair-minded warning

"Till, when they came to the valley of the ants, one of the ants said: 'O ants! Enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his armies should crush you, while they perceive not.'"

The verb is the language of being crushed — the ordinary, unnoticed fate of an ant beneath a marching column. But look at the clause the ant adds: **"while they perceive not."** She warns her people and, in the same breath, clears the marchers of blame. There is no accusation in it. The danger is real, so take shelter; but no injustice is intended, because they are simply unaware.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a question this raises — do animals have understanding? Its answer is measured: there is sense and intelligence to some degree in all animals and birds, but not developed to the point where they are made to follow the injunctions of the Sharīʿah. Human beings and jinn are the ones bestowed with intelligence so perfected that they are made the addressees and followers of Allah's commands. So the ant's speech is not a fable of animals as moral agents; it is a window onto a creation more aware than we assume.

The commentary supports this with observations from the scholars: Imam Shāfiʿī said the dove is the cleverest of all the birds, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said the ant is a very intelligent animal with a very strong sense of smell — when it takes hold of a grain it breaks it in two so that it will not germinate, and in this way stocks its food for the winter.

## Ayah 19: the smile, and the prayer of a grateful king

"So he smiled, amused at her speech." Ibn Kathir states the fact that makes the moment possible: Sulayman, peace be upon him, understood what the ant said. The Arabic *fa-tabassama ḍāḥikan* is a smile — delight breaking across the face of a man at the head of an army of humans, jinn and birds, because a single ant took him seriously enough to organise an evacuation, and generously enough to say he meant no harm.

And then the prayer. It is the sequence that is remarkable: not a command, not a boast, but a request — as though the sight of a creature so small handling its responsibilities so well made him instantly aware of how much he had been given and how easily gratitude could slip.

**"My Lord, *awziʿnī* — enable me — that I may be grateful."** Here the earlier word returns. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *awziʿnī* is derived from that same *wazʿ*, to stop or restrain: the meaning is, *enable me by Your help to have the trait of gratitude with me all the time and never to part with it* — which amounts to a restraint placed on the self, the way *yūzaʿūn* in ayah 17 was a restraint placed on the ranks. Sulayman could keep an army of jinn and men and birds from breaking formation. He is asking Allah to do that for his own heart. Ibn Kathir gives the sense of the request as: *inspire me to give thanks for the blessings You have bestowed on me* — by teaching me to understand what the birds and animals say.

**"…and on my parents."** Ibn Kathir explains the blessing on his parents as this: that Allah made them Muslims who believed in Him. Of everything Sulayman could name about Dawud — the kingdom, the prophethood, the craft of armour — the favour he singles out for thanks is faith.

**"…and that I may do righteous good deeds that will please You."** Ibn Kathir: deeds that You love, which will earn Your pleasure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further on *tarḍāhu*: here "pleasure" carries the sense of **acceptance**, so the request is, *grace me with Your help for such righteous deeds as are acceptable to You.* From this, it notes (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī), it is argued that a deed being righteous does not by itself guarantee that it is accepted; acceptance depends on certain conditions, and there is no relation between righteousness and acceptance either rationally or in religious law. That is precisely why the prophets used to pray for the acceptance of their righteous deeds: Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl, while constructing the House of Allah, prayed *"Our Lord, accept from us"* (2:127). **The practical upshot, as Maʿārif draws it: after doing a good deed, do not settle back complacent with it — pray to Allah for its acceptance.**

**"…and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a prayer for the end: *when You cause me to die, join me with the righteous among Your servants, and with the Higher Companion among Your close friends.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the word *bi-raḥmatika*, "by Your mercy." Even with righteous deeds done and accepted, entry into Paradise will depend on the grace and kindness of Allah. It cites the Prophet ﷺ as having said that no one will enter Paradise relying only on his deeds; the Companions asked, "Even you too?" and he answered, "Yes, me too, but I am surrounded by Allah's favour and grace." So Sulayman, the commentary says, was asking for the very same thing: *O Allah, grace me too with Your favour, so that I may become entitled to enter Paradise.*

Note the shape of the whole du'a: gratitude for the past, righteous action in the present, and mercy for the outcome. Nothing in it is a claim; every clause begins from need.

## Living it

**Rank knowledge first.** The passage opens with knowledge before kingdom, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from Qurtubi, reads that order as a clear hint that knowledge is the paramount blessing of them all. What we spend our lives acquiring should reflect that order.

**Know what is worth inheriting.** The Prophet ﷺ taught, as Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report from Abū Dardāʾ, that the people of knowledge are the inheritors of the prophets, and that what the prophets left was not dirhams and dinars but knowledge. The estate worth entering is open to anyone willing to learn.

**Let blessings trigger praise, not swagger.** Every gift in this passage is named together with its Giver — *al-hamdu lillah* in ayah 15, "an evident grace" in ayah 16, and in ayah 19 a plea for the strength to keep giving thanks.

**Be like the ant's warning.** She protected her own without accusing anyone: real danger named honestly, and the benefit of the doubt extended — "while they perceive not."

**Thank Allah for your parents' faith.** That is the favour Sulayman singled out, on Ibn Kathir's reading, while riding at the head of his hosts.

**Ask for acceptance, and lean on mercy.** Pray as Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl did — "Our Lord, accept from us" — and let your hope of Paradise rest where Sulayman rested his: on *"by Your mercy."*

passages.title: The hoopoe's report on the sun-worshipping queen
passages.tafsir:
A king inspects his troops, notices one small bird missing, and that single act of attention sets in motion the story of a whole nation's turn to Allah. These seven ayat run from Sulayman's roll-call of the birds (ayah 20) to the hoopoe's report about a sun-worshipping queen in Yemen — a report that ends not with politics but with the declaration of Allah's oneness (ayah 26).

What holds the passage together is one movement: **a small absence is noticed, investigated, and turns out to carry news of tawhid** — tawhid being the affirmation that Allah alone is to be worshipped.

## Ayah 20: "What is wrong with **me**?"

The verb is وَتَفَقَّدَ (*tafaqqada*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *tafaqqud* means to verify who is present and who is absent — hence "he checked" or "he inspected."

Allah had given Sulayman (peace be upon him) rule not only over people but over the jinn, the beasts and the birds. Maʿārif notes that it is customary for a ruler to look after and take care of all his subjects — and this ayah shows Sulayman taking note of the presence and absence of them all, so that the absence of one hoopoe, a bird small and weak with a small population compared with other birds, did not go unnoticed. Maʿārif even suggests his particular enquiry about the hoopoe may have been *because* of its small population and weak make-up — that he made a special effort to keep his eye on the weaker section of his subjects.

Maʿārif then draws the line forward to our own Prophet ﷺ, who kept himself informed about the wellbeing of his Companions: if someone was absent he would go to his house to find out his welfare; if someone was sick he would visit him and do the needful nursing; if someone was afflicted with any trouble he would make the effort to remove it. And forward again to Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), who went round the streets of Madinah at night to keep himself fully abreast of the state of affairs, helping out anyone he found in distress or need. Maʿārif cites Qurtubi for his famous words: "If a wolf kills a lamb by the side of river Euphrates, for that too ʿUmar will be answerable."

Apparently, as Maʿārif puts it, Sulayman should have said, "What is wrong with the hoopoe that he is absent?" Instead he says, *mā liya lā arā al-hudhud* — "What is wrong with **me** that I do not see the hoopoe?" Maʿārif offers a beautiful reading: the hoopoe and all the other birds had been put under his control as a special reward, and it crossed his mind momentarily that perhaps that blessing had been curtailed because of some slip on his own part.

Maʿārif compares this to the way of the mystic saints, who make enquiries of their own selves before looking into material causes when distress comes or a blessing is reduced — taking account of any slip on their part in thanking Allah for His bounties. Maʿārif quotes Qurtubi, on the authority of Ibn al-ʿArabī:

> *idhā faqadū āmālahum tafaqqadū aʿmālahum* — "when these saints do not succeed in their objectives, they take stock of their deeds to find out where they have committed the mistake."

Then comes أَمْ كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْغَائِبِينَ. Here, Maʿārif reports from Qurtubi, the word *am* is used with the meaning of *bal* — "rather." So the sense is: *it is not that my sight has faltered in locating the hoopoe; rather, he is in fact not present.*

## Why a hoopoe at all?

Ibn Kathir reports — from Mujahid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others, from Ibn ʿAbbās and others — that the hoopoe was an expert who used to show Sulayman where water was when he was out in open land and needed it. The hoopoe would look for water in the various strata of the earth and would know just how far below the surface the water lay. Once he showed the place, Sulayman would command the jinn to dig there until they brought the water up from the depths.

Ibn ʿAbbās was telling this story when among the people was a man of the Khawārij named Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, who often used to raise objections to him. He said, "Stop, O Ibn ʿAbbās; you will be defeated today!" His objection was sharp: if the hoopoe can see water beneath the ground, how is it that any boy can put seed in a trap, cover the trap with dirt, and catch the bird when it comes for the seed? Ibn ʿAbbās said that if it were not for the fact that this man would go and tell others he had defeated Ibn ʿAbbās in argument, he would not even answer. Then he said:

> "Woe to you! When the decree strikes a person, his eyes become blind and he loses all caution."

Nāfiʿ said: "By Allah, I will never dispute with you concerning anything in the Qur'an."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same point from Ibn ʿAbbās, addressed to the people of knowledge: the hoopoe has the ability to see things under the ground, but the net spread out over the ground is obscured from its sight, and so it is caught. Maʿārif draws the lesson plainly: **whatever is destined for a person by the divine decree, whether trouble or comfort, has to come to pass; no one escapes it by wisdom, insight, force or money.**

## Ayah 21: the threat, and the door left open

On the "severe torment," Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās (al-Aʿmash narrating from al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr from Saʿīd) that it meant plucking his feathers. ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaddād said: plucking his feathers and exposing him to the sun; and Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of more than one of the Salaf — that it means plucking his feathers and leaving him exposed to be eaten by ants. "Or I will slaughter him" means, simply, killing him.

The third clause, أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطَانٍ مُبِينٍ — "unless he brings me a clear reason" — means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, **a valid excuse**. Ibn Kathir relates from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah and ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaddād that when the hoopoe came back, the other birds said to him: "What kept you? Sulayman has vowed to shed your blood!" The hoopoe asked, "Did he make any exception?" They said yes — he said *"unless he brings me a clear reason."* The hoopoe replied: **"Then I am saved."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two rulings from the ayah:

**Governance.** It is part of political sagacity to punish an absentee only after due scrutiny. There is a subtle hint here that a ruler or administrator, when someone falters, should investigate thoroughly before punishing; the punishment is enforced only when the guilt is established, and otherwise the person should be forgiven.

**Animals.** Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, explains that Allah had permitted Sulayman to punish animals in this way, just as He has permitted people of all ages — a permission still valid — to slaughter them and make use of their flesh, bones and skin. Similarly, if a domestic animal such as a cow, horse, camel or donkey does not perform its normal duty, it is permissible even now to discipline it *moderately*. Punishing animals other than domestic ones is not permissible under Islamic law.

## Ayah 22: the absence was short, and the news was certain

فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ — "he stayed not long." Ibn Kathir: he was absent for only a short time.

Then the bird speaks: أَحَطتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *"I have come to know something that you and your troops do not know."*

Maʿārif reports that Imam Qurtubi deduced from this very incident that the prophets do not have knowledge of the unseen (*ʿilm al-ghayb*) such that they would know all about everything — it is quite evident from this ayah.

Maʿārif also raises a question of manners: is it proper for a junior to tell a senior that he knows more than him? Some have deduced from the hoopoe's words that a pupil may say this to his teacher, or a common man to a knowledgeable person, provided he is absolutely confident. But Maʿārif cites *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: such an assertion before elders and scholars is against the etiquettes and should be avoided. The hoopoe's case is different — it made that statement to save itself from punishment and to justify its excuse, and it wanted to place the exact position before Sulayman so he could understand the reason for its absence. **In such situations, Maʿārif concludes, it is not improper if something is said against the normal etiquettes.**

*Wa ji'tuka min Saba'in bi-naba'in yaqīn* — "and I have come to you from Saba' with true news." Ibn Kathir explains this as true and certain news, and says Saba' (Sheba) refers to Ḥimyar, a dynasty in Yemen. Maʿārif adds that Saba' is a well-known city of Yemen whose other name is Ma'ārib, and that the distance between Sanʿā', the capital of Yemen, and Saba' is three days' journey.

## Ayat 23–24: the queen, the throne, and the sun

Ibn Kathir cites al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "This is Bilqīs bint Sharāḥīl, the queen of Saba'." Maʿārif gives the same name from history, and adds that in some other narrations her mother was a jinn woman named Balʿamah bint Shīsān — Wuhaib ibn Jarīr reported this from Khalīl ibn Aḥmad (Qurtubi). Maʿārif further relates that her grandfather, Hudhud, was a great king who controlled the entire land of Yemen and had forty sons who all became kings, and that her father, Surah, married a jinn woman who gave birth to Bilqīs. One reason given for that marriage, which Maʿārif attributes to Qurtubi, is that he used to say arrogantly, "No one among you is a match for me; hence I will not marry, for I do not like marrying outside my matching clan" — and so people got him married to a jinn woman. Maʿārif comments that perhaps it was his conceit in deeming his own people not his equal; this did not go well with the Divine writ, and he was made to marry someone who was neither of his family nor his kind or race.

On whether a man may marry a jinn woman, Maʿārif reports that some doubted it on the assumption that jinn cannot reproduce as humans do, and that Ibn al-ʿArabī held this to be a wrong conception, since it is established that jinn possess the requisites of reproduction as humans do. The jurists differed: some held it permissible, others ruled it out on the grounds of difference of kind. But Maʿārif then closes the door on drawing any ruling from this passage: Bilqīs's father, who married the jinn woman, was not a Muslim, so the question of permissibility does not arise; and since in Islamic law lineage is based on the father, and her father was human, **Bilqīs herself is regarded as a human being.** As for the narrations that Sulayman later married her, even if correct they would not corroborate the permissibility of marrying a jinn woman, since Bilqīs was not one, though her mother might have been — and Maʿārif closes with *Allah knows best*.

**Can a woman be head of state?** Maʿārif reports from Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), that when the Prophet ﷺ learnt that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Kisrā their queen, he said: *"Those people will never prosper who give control of authority to a woman."* On the basis of this verdict, Maʿārif states, the scholars are unanimous that the control of a government, an empire or the caliphate cannot be assigned to a woman; rather the greater imamate (*al-imāmah al-kubrā*) is allowed only to men, like the imamate for prayers. And Maʿārif is careful about arguing from this ayah: that Bilqīs was queen of Saba' does not by itself make a religious decree; it could only become one if it were proven that Sulayman married her and *then retained* her as queen — and that assumption, Maʿārif says, is not proven by any authentic narration that could be trusted for legislating religious law.

*Wa ūtiyat min kulli shay'* — Ibn Kathir: she had been given all the conveniences of this world that a powerful monarch could need. Maʿārif adds: it means whatever services a king or aristocrat of that time required; things not yet invented then are obviously no contradiction to the verse.

*Wa lahā ʿarshun ʿaẓīm* — Ibn Kathir describes a tremendous chair adorned with gold and different kinds of jewels and pearls. Maʿārif notes that the literal meaning of *ʿarsh* is the throne of the empire, and reports a narration attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās giving its dimensions as eighty yards long, forty broad and thirty high, profusely decorated with pearls, red rubies, topaz and olivine, its legs studded with precious stones and pearls, its curtains of silk and fine cloth, and the whole secured within seven buildings set one within another, all protected and locked.

**The palace of windows.** Ibn Kathir reports from the historians that the throne stood in a great, strong palace, high and firmly constructed, with three hundred and sixty windows on the east side and a similar number on the west, built so that each day the rising sun would shine through one window and the setting sun through the opposite one. Morning and evening, the people prostrated to the sun.

*Wa zayyana lahum al-shayṭānu aʿmālahum* — "and Shayṭān has made their deeds fair-seeming to them, and has prevented them from the way." Ibn Kathir: from the way of truth — *fahum lā yahtadūn*, so they have no guidance. Maʿārif notes these people were star-worshippers who worshipped the sun; some believe they were Zoroastrians, who worship fire and all forms of light.

## Ayat 25–26: the correction — bow to the One who made it

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 25 as continuing directly from the beautification: because Shayṭān made their deeds fair-seeming and prevented them from the way, **they do not prostrate themselves before Allah.** Maʿārif states the connection the same way: Shayṭān had engrained in their minds that they should not bow down before Allah, or had prevented them from the righteous path so that they would not prostrate to Him.

Ibn Kathir: they do not know the way of truth, which is to prostrate before Allah alone and not before anything He has created, whether heavenly bodies or anything else. He brings the parallel ayah: *"And from among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Prostrate yourselves not to the sun nor to the moon, but prostrate yourselves to Allah Who created them, if you indeed worship Him."* (41:37) The sun is not a rival to Allah; it is one of His signs.

Then the ayah names Allah by two descriptions that answer sun-worship exactly:

**الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الْخَبْءَ — "Who brings to light what is hidden in the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir cites ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās: "He knows everything that is hidden in the heavens and on earth" — and this was also the view of ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah and others. A people who bowed to the most visible thing in the sky are told that the One deserving their prostration is the One who brings forth what is hidden.

**وَيَعْلَمُ مَا تُخْفُونَ وَمَا تُعْلِنُونَ — "and knows what you conceal and what you reveal."** Ibn Kathir: He knows what His servants say and do in secret, and what they say and do openly, as in: *"It is the same whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he be hid by night or goes forth freely by day."* (13:10)

And then ayah 26, the summit: **ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ رَبُّ ٱلْعَرْشِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ ۩.** Ibn Kathir explains: He is the One to be called upon; He is the One other than whom there is no god, the Lord of the Supreme Throne — **and there is none greater than Him in all of creation.** In the muṣḥaf this ayah carries the sign of prostration (۩): a passage that opened with a nation bowing to the sun brings the reciter's own forehead to the ground before Allah.

## What the passage asks of us

**Notice who is missing.** Sulayman's greatness here is not only that he commanded jinn and birds, but that he counted the smallest one. Maʿārif applies this directly: it is necessary for rulers to take care of their subjects, and for the saints to take care of their disciples and students — with particular attention, as Sulayman showed, to the weaker section among them.

**Blame yourself first, and hear the other side.** *"What is wrong with me?"* is a whole spiritual method in a few words: when something is withdrawn, take stock of your own deeds before you audit the world. And note that the oath in ayah 21 always contained an exception — the accused was heard before sentence was passed, which is exactly the principle Maʿārif draws out for anyone in authority.

**Suspect what merely looks beautiful.** Their error had been made fair-seeming to them by Shayṭān. So the question to ask of any practice is not only "does this feel right?" but "to whom, in the end, does this make me bow?"

**Carry the message, whoever you are.** Ibn Kathir closes with an extraordinary observation: since the hoopoe was calling to what is good, and calling people to worship and prostrate to Allah alone, it would have been forbidden to kill him. And he records that Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ forbade killing four kinds of animals: ants, bees, hoopoes and the sparrow hawks — Ibn Kathir notes that its chain of narration is *ṣaḥīḥ*. The bird who returned with a word of tawhid did not merely escape the sword; his whole kind was placed under protection.

passages.title: Solomon's letter delivered to Sheba's queen
passages.tafsir:
A hoopoe has just come back to Sulayman (peace be upon him) with news of a distant kingdom in Saba' (Sheba) ruled by a queen whose people prostrate to the sun. These five ayat are Sulayman's response: he refuses to act on an unverified report, writes a short letter, and sends it by bird — and we watch it land in the queen's chamber and be read aloud to her court. What holds the passage together is a single object: **the letter**. Ayah 27 is the decision to send it, ayah 28 the commission to carry it, ayah 29 the queen's reaction to receiving it, and ayat 30–31 its actual text, quoted word for word.

## Ayah 27 — a king who checks before he acts

Sulayman does not accept the hoopoe's report simply because it is dramatic, and he does not punish the bird simply because it went missing. He says: *"We shall see whether you speak the truth or you are one of the liars."*

Ibn Kathir explains the two halves plainly. *"We shall see whether you speak the truth"* means: are you telling the truth? And *"or you are one of the liars"* means: or are you telling a lie in order to save yourself from the threat I made against you. That second reading is important — it shows Sulayman is alive to the possibility that a convenient story has been produced under pressure. The report may be true; it may also be a bird talking its way out of trouble. Either way, the verdict waits.

Notice what he does not do: he does not act against Saba' on the strength of an unchecked report, nor does he shrug the news off. He says *we shall see* — and then, in the very next ayah, sets about seeing.

## Ayah 28 — the commission, and the manners inside it

*"Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then draw back from them and see what they return."*

Three instructions, in order. **Deliver.** **Withdraw.** **Watch.**

**Deliver — and the standing of a written document.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a fiqh point (a point of Islamic law) from the simple word *bi-kitābī* ("with this letter of mine"): Sulayman considered a written letter sufficient to discharge his duty of calling the queen of Saba' to faith. This shows that in ordinary circumstances a letter or a piece of writing is acceptable proof. The one place the jurists did not accept it is where formal personal testimony is required under Islamic law — a witness may not testify by letter or by telephone but must appear in person before the court. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there is much wisdom in this, and that legal systems everywhere likewise require witnesses to attend in person.

A second ruling follows from the same word: it is permissible, in calling people to Allah, to write letters to disbelievers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that many rigorously authenticated reports establish that the Prophet ﷺ also wrote letters to many disbelievers.

**Withdraw — good manners even in a hostile court.** *"Then draw back from them"* is read by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as Sulayman teaching his courier the etiquette of a royal court — after delivering the letter, the messenger steps out of the queen's presence, as the norm of royal courts requires. From this the commentary draws a general rule: the observance of social etiquette and good conduct is desirable as a general principle, and it does not lapse because the gathering is a gathering of unbelievers. Calling people to Allah is not an excuse for rudeness.

**Watch — *fa-nẓur mādhā yarjiʿūn*, "then see what they return."** The last instruction is not to argue in person but to observe the answer that comes back.

### The delivery itself

Ibn Kathir relates what was said about how it happened. Sulayman wrote the letter to Bilqis and her people and gave it to the hoopoe. It was said that the bird carried it on its wings, as is the way with birds, or that it carried it in its beak. The hoopoe went to their land, found the palace of Bilqis, made its way to her private chambers, threw the letter through a small window — and then stepped to one side, out of good manners. Bilqis was amazed and confused by what she saw. Then she went, picked up the letter, opened its seal, and read it.

That small detail — the bird that delivers and then steps aside — is the hinge of what happens next.

## Ayah 29 — "a noble letter"

She gathers her commanders, her ministers and the leaders of her land, and announces: *"O chiefs! Verily, here is delivered to me a noble letter."*

**Why "noble"?** Ibn Kathir says she described it that way because of the wondrous things she had seen: that it was delivered by a bird, which threw it to her and then stood aside out of good manners — something no king could do. The letter announced itself before a word of it was read.

**The word *karīm*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the literal sense of *karīm* is respectable, honourable, esteemed — but that idiomatically the word is used of a letter when it is **sealed**. On that basis Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Zuhayr understood *kitāb karīm* as the sealed letter, which indicates that Sulayman had put his seal on it.

This connects directly to the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when he ﷺ learned that the non-Arab kings would not read a letter that was not sealed, he had a seal made for himself and used it on the letters he sent to Caesar and Chosroes. Sealing, then, shows respect both for the letter and for the person receiving it. The commentary adds the modern equivalent: securing a letter in an envelope is as good as sealing it, and where respect for the addressee is intended, using an envelope is closer to the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.

**What language was it in?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, weighs the possibilities. Sulayman was not an Arab, yet it is not unlikely that he knew Arabic — especially given that he knew the languages of the animals. Since Arabic is supreme among languages, it is possible he wrote in Arabic; this is also made probable by the fact that Bilqis was an Arab by race, and she read the letter and understood it. The other possibility is that he wrote in his own language and an interpreter read it out to her.

## Ayat 30–31 — the letter itself

*"Verily, it is from Sulayman, and it reads: 'In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Be you not exalted against me, but come to me submitting (as Muslims).'"*

Ibn Kathir's verdict on it is one line and it is worth remembering: **this letter was the utmost in brevity and eloquence, coming straight to the point.** When she read it out, he says, they knew it was from Allah's Prophet Sulayman, upon him be peace, and that they could not match him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks what is packed into those few words: all the important matters are put together in a few sentences; the high standard of eloquence is maintained; royal grandeur is kept up before disbelievers; the perfected attributes of Allah are described; there is an invitation to Islam; and conceit and arrogance are condemned — all at once. It calls the letter a specimen of the marvel of the Qur'an. Qatadah stated that it was the practice of all the prophets in letter-writing to be brief while ensuring that nothing worth mentioning was left out.

### "Be you not exalted against me"

*Allā taʿlū ʿalayya.* Ibn Kathir reports Qatadah's gloss: **"Do not be arrogant with me."** ʿAbd ar-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam reads it as: "Do not refuse or be too arrogant to come to me."

So the first demand is the removal of an obstacle. Before *come*, there is *do not be exalted against me*. The sun-worship the hoopoe reported was bound up, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains on the preceding ayat, with Shaytan having beautified their deeds — he had so worked on their minds that they would not bow down before Allah, the One who brings forth what is hidden. Arrogance is what stands between them and that prostration, and the letter names it first.

### "…but come to me submitting"

*Wa'tūnī muslimīn.* The word is *muslimīn* — those who submit. The invitation is not "become my subjects" but "come submitted to Allah". A whole religion is offered in two words, and it is offered to a queen at the height of her power.

## What this letter teaches about writing to people

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats these two ayat as a model, since the Qur'an has reproduced a prophet's letter in full and so has given us an approved format for correspondence, which Muslims should try to follow. The points it draws out:

**Name yourself first.** Sulayman began by writing his own name. How he wrote the name of the addressee is not mentioned in the Qur'an — but it tells us that the practice of the prophets was to write their own name first, and the benefits are many: the reader knows who is writing before reading a word, and reads it in the light of his relationship with the writer, with any confusion about the writer's identity removed at the outset. The Prophet ﷺ followed the same practice in all his letters, opening with *min Muḥammad ʿabdillāhi wa rasūlih* — "From Muhammad, the slave of Allah and His Messenger."

**Is that disrespectful when writing to an elder?** The Companions did not all act identically. Most preferred to follow the practice of the Prophet ﷺ over the demands of formality, and wrote their own names first even when writing to him ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites, through Rūḥ al-Maʿānī from al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, a narration of Anas: no one was more revered than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, yet when his Companions wrote to him they would begin with their own names — and the letter of ʿAlā' al-Ḥaḍramī to the Prophet ﷺ is cited as a proof of that. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī then observes that this whole discussion concerns only the *preferred* way: both ways are permissible, and writing one's own name last is also correct. The jurist Abu al-Layth wrote in his *Bustān* that no one can question the permissibility of beginning with the addressee's name, since this too has long been the practice among Muslims without objection.

**Begin with Bismillah.** Sulayman's letter and all the letters of the Prophet ﷺ establish that writing Bismillah at the beginning of a letter was the practice of the prophets. Should Bismillah come before the writer's name? The practice of the Prophet ﷺ was to put Bismillah first, then his own name, then the addressee's — while in the Qur'an's wording here the order is reversed, Sulayman's name and then Bismillah; so writing one's own name first and Bismillah after is also in order.

But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags a genuine difference over what the original letter looked like. Ibn Abi Hatim reported, on the authority of Yazid ibn Rūmān, that Sulayman in fact wrote his letter in this manner: *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm — from Sulayman son of Dawud to Bilqis daughter of Sharḥ and her people: be you not exalted against me, but come to me submitting* — that is, Bismillah before his name — and that when Bilqis read it out to her people she mentioned Sulayman's name first in order to let them know who had written it, and the Qur'an has copied what **she** uttered. There is no mention in the Qur'an of which came first in the original letter. A further possibility is that Sulayman's name was written on the envelope and Bismillah at the head of the letter, and Bilqis announced the writer's name first.

**A ruling for our own time.** The original Sunnah of letter-writing is that all letters should begin with Bismillah. But the jurists have ruled, on the indications given in the Qur'an and Sunnah, that where there is a risk of disrespect to the name of Allah — the paper it is written on being thrown away — it is not right to write it, lest one fall into sin. Since letters today are commonly discarded and end up in the rubbish, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds it better to fulfil the Sunnah by **saying** Bismillah aloud before beginning to write, rather than putting it on the paper.

**May a paper bearing Qur'anic words be handed to a non-Muslim?** Sulayman sent this letter to Bilqis while she was not a Muslim, and *Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm* was written on it — which confirms that this is permissible. The non-Arab kings the Prophet ﷺ wrote to were disbelievers, and his letters contained some Qur'anic verses too. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the principle: while the Qur'an itself may not be handed over to a disbeliever, any book or paper containing some verses of the Qur'an does not thereby qualify as the Qur'an itself, and so such papers or books may be given to a non-Muslim, or to someone who is not in a state of wudu' (ablution) — citing *ʿĀlamgīrī*.

**Answer the letters you receive.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: if someone receives a letter, it is incumbent upon him to answer it, because a letter from someone who is absent is as good as the greeting of one who is present. It is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas in a narration that he regarded replying to a letter as much an obligation as returning the greeting of salām.

## Living it

Four things this passage asks of us, in the order it gives them:

1. **Verify before you act on a report** — ayah 27. Even when the news comes from a trusted source and even when it is exciting, Sulayman's *"we shall see"* is the believer's default.
2. **Keep your manners in rooms that do not share your faith** — ayah 28. The courier was taught court etiquette before it was sent. Good conduct, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is desirable as a general rule — it is not a reward for agreement.
3. **Say it short and say it whole** — ayat 30–31. Qatadah's description of prophetic letters is a standard for every message we send: brief, but leaving out nothing worth mentioning.
4. **Deal with arrogance before anything else** — ayah 31. *Be you not exalted against me* comes before *come to me submitting*. That order is as true of our own hearts as it was of the court of Saba'.

passages.title: The queen's council, her gift, and its refusal
passages.tafsir:
Sulayman's letter has reached Queen Bilqīs, and this passage is her reply — not in words at first, but in strategy. Across ayat 32–37 we watch a shrewd ruler gather her council, weigh war against diplomacy, and send a caravan of treasure as a test; and we watch that test come back to her undelivered, with a message that leaves her only two roads. What holds the passage together is a single question that never quite gets asked aloud: **is this man a king, or is he a prophet?** Everything the queen does is designed to find out, and everything Sulayman does answers her.

## A ruler who will not decide alone (ayah 32)

Her first move is not military. It is consultative. "O chiefs! Advise me in this matter of mine; I decide no case till you are present with me."

The word she uses for "advise me" is **aftūnī** (أفتوني), which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains is derived from **fatwā** — answering some specific issue put to you. Here, it says, the word means to give counsel, to express one's views on the case in hand. She is not asking for applause. She is putting a file on the table and asking for rulings.

Notice the order of her sentence, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to: *before* she asks their opinion, she reassures them — "I am not the one who decides a matter absolutely unless you are present with me." She encouraged and pleased them first by declaring that she did not take decisions without consulting them. The effect was immediate: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that because of her remarks, the ministers and the generals expressed their readiness to sacrifice everything they had in order to follow her command. In ayah 33 they answer: "We have great strength, and great ability for war — but it is for you to command; so think over what you will command."

Ibn Kathir reads their reply as two moves in one. First they remind her of their great numbers, their preparedness and their strength — meaning, as he puts it, *we have the power and strength, if you want to go to him and fight him.* Then they hand the decision straight back: the matter is yours to decide, so instruct us as you see fit and we will obey. That is a council offering capability without seizing authority — which is exactly what good counsel looks like.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Qatādah, citing Qurṭubī, that there were 313 members in her consultative committee, each of whom represented and enjoyed the support of ten thousand persons. Whatever the exact figure, the picture is of a governing assembly, not a handful of courtiers.

## Consultation is an old practice, and Islam made it binding

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here for a principle that reaches far beyond her court: **consultation in important matters is a Sunnah.** It provides the benefit of having the views of others, and it gives them a sense of participation. This statement, it says, brings to light that having consultation with supporters is an old practice — and Islam attached great importance to it and made it mandatory for those who hold government responsibility.

Then comes the striking part of the argument. The Prophet ﷺ received revelation from Allah and direct guidance from Him — so, strictly speaking, he had no need of consultation or advice. Yet he was still commanded to follow this practice, in order to set up a tradition for his followers: **وَشَاوِرْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ** — "and consult them in the matter" (3:159). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wisdom: there is a sense of participation for the Companions in this command, and an advice for the coming generations that those in public office must always consult on important matters.

So the lesson is not merely that a clever idolatrous queen happened to be a good manager. It is that Allah preserved her method in His Book, and then made that method binding practice for the leaders of this Ummah.

## "Kings, when they enter a town, ruin it" (ayah 34)

Her council has offered her war. She declines it — and her reasoning in ayah 34 is one of the most quoted political observations in the Qurʼān: "Verily, kings, when they enter a town, they destroy it and make the most honourable among its people the lowest."

Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās for the point that this sentence is hers — the queen's own read on how conquest works. And then he marks off the closing clause, **وَكَذَٰلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ** ("And thus they do"), as Allah's own words rather than part of her speech. A woman raised in idolatry says something true about the world, and it stands in the Book of Allah confirmed. Truth is not made true by the one who says it.

Her conclusion is not surrender but de-escalation. Ibn Kathir says she then "resorted to peaceful means, seeking a truce and trying to placate Sulayman."

## The gift that was really a question (ayah 35)

"But verily, I am going to send him a present, and see with what the messengers return."

Ibn Kathir gives her calculation in plain terms: *I will send him a gift befitting one of his status, and will wait and see what his response will be. Perhaps he will accept that and leave us alone, or he will impose a tax which we can pay him every year, so that he will not fight us and wage war against us.*
